summary: Defines an extensible way to return extra information about why a DNS error occurred. It was created mainly to extend SERVFAIL with details about DNS and DNSSEC failures, but any response type can carry extended error information. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: When a DNS lookup fails, the answer used to be just "it didn't work". This adds a reason, like a note saying why, so people can fix the problem faster.

questions: why did my dns lookup return servfail
what does dnssec bogus ede mean
subtitle: A way for DNS servers to say why a query failed, not just that it failed.

tldr.problem: DNS error signals such as SERVFAIL are very limited, so applications and resolvers have to guess whether a failure was a DNSSEC validation problem, a server still starting up, or something else.
tldr.mechanism: An EDNS0 option, the Extended DNS Error (EDE) option, carries a 16-bit INFO-CODE from a new IANA registry plus optional human-readable EXTRA-TEXT, attached to any response to a query that included an OPT pseudo-RR.
tldr.outcome: EDE is diagnostic only: it does not change how RCODEs are processed, and because it is unauthenticated unless the transaction is secured it must not alter DNS protocol processing.

today: RFC 8914 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2020. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why DNS Errors Need More Detail
sections.content:
A DNS query can fail for many reasons: some transient, some permanent, some fixable by asking another server. The error signals a DNS server can return are very limited, so applications and resolvers often have to guess. Was a REFUSED caused by a lame delegation or by a nameserver that is still loading zones? Is a SERVFAIL a DNSSEC validation issue or some other failure?

The RFC's main example is DNSSEC. When a stub resolver asks a validating resolver for a name that is DNSSEC bogus, it receives only a SERVFAIL. Its only option is to ask the next configured resolver. That resolver either also validates and fails again, or does not validate and the user gets a potentially harmful result.

RFC 8914 defines the Extended DNS Error (EDE) option so a response can carry a more descriptive reason, or add context even to a message with a NOERROR RCODE. Any system that sends DNS queries and receives a response containing an EDE option can use the codes: stub, recursive and authoritative servers all may see them.
sections.eli5: Imagine a vending machine that only ever shows "ERROR". This gives it a little screen that says "out of change" or "sold out", so you know what to do next.

sections.title: The EDE Option Format
sections.content:
EDE is carried as an EDNS0 option. The option has four parts: OPTION-CODE, OPTION-LENGTH, INFO-CODE and EXTRA-TEXT.

  • OPTION-CODE is 16 bits and contains the value 15 for EDE.
  • OPTION-LENGTH is 16 bits and holds the length of everything after it in octets. It should be 2 plus the length of EXTRA-TEXT, which may be a zero-length string.
  • INFO-CODE is 16 bits in network byte order. It adds context to the message's RESPONSE-CODE and acts as an index into the Extended DNS Errors registry.
  • EXTRA-TEXT is variable-length UTF-8 text meant for humans, not automated parsing. It may be null terminated but MUST NOT be assumed to be, so the length MUST be derived from OPTION-LENGTH.

Care should be taken not to put private information in EXTRA-TEXT that an observer would not otherwise have access to, such as account numbers. The option can appear in any response (SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, REFUSED, even NOERROR) to a query that includes an OPT pseudo-RR.
sections.eli5: The note has a label saying "this is an error note", a length, a number that says which kind of problem it is, and optionally a few words in plain language.

sections.title: How EDE Is Processed
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD truncate an oversized response by dropping EDE options before dropping other data, and SHOULD set the truncation bit when they do. Because long EXTRA-TEXT may trigger truncation, implementers and operators SHOULD avoid lengthy EXTRA-TEXT.

When a resolver or forwarder receives an EDE option, whether and how to pass it on is implementation dependent. It MAY drop it or create new EDE options conveying the same information. If it does, the source of the error SHOULD be attributed in EXTRA-TEXT, because the original client will see the option as coming from the resolver or forwarder.

The RFC does not allow or prohibit any pairing of extended codes with RCODEs, so receivers MUST NOT assume a combination makes sense. Receivers MUST be able to accept EDE codes and EXTRA-TEXT in all messages, including NOERROR ones, but need not act on them. Applications MUST continue to follow the normal rules for RCODEs whatever EDE values arrive. Senders MAY include more than one EDE option, and receivers MUST accept multiple options.
sections.eli5: The note is extra help, not an order. If space is tight, the note is the first thing thrown out, and nobody should change what they do just because of what the note says.

sections.title: The Initial Error Codes
sections.content:
The RFC defines codes 0 to 24. They fall into a few groups.

  • DNSSEC validation: codes 1, 2, 5 to 12 cover unsupported algorithms or digest types, Indeterminate and Bogus states, expired or not-yet-valid signatures, and missing DNSKEY, RRSIG or NSEC records.
  • Stale and cached data: Stale Answer (3) and Stale NXDOMAIN Answer (19) mean the resolver answered from cache because it could not resolve in time, and Cached Error (13) means a SERVFAIL came from the cache.
  • Policy: Forged Answer (4) is used when an answer was still provided. Blocked (15), Censored (16) and Filtered (17) distinguish a blocklist from the operator's own policy, an external requirement, or the client's request. Prohibited (18) annotates a REFUSED for an unauthorized client.
  • Server state and reachability: Not Ready (14), Not Authoritative (20), Not Supported (21), No Reachable Authority (22), Network Error (23) and Invalid Data (24).

Code 0, Other, is for errors that match none of the known codes, and implementations SHOULD include EXTRA-TEXT with it.
sections.eli5: There is a menu of reasons: the lock on the answer was broken, the answer is old, someone blocked this on purpose, or the server just was not ready.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned EDNS0 option value 15, named "Extended DNS Error" with status Standard, in the "DNS EDNS0 Option Codes (OPT)" registry.

It also created the "Extended DNS Error Codes" registry. Codes 0 to 49151 are First Come First Served, and 49152 to 65535 are Private Use. The initial contents are the codes defined in the previous section, with 25 to 49151 unassigned.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of reason numbers. Most numbers can be claimed by asking first, and a block at the end is left for anyone's private use.

sections.title: Security of Error Information
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a significant number of clients (about 11% according to the cited measurement) that get a SERVFAIL from a validating resolver will simply ask the next, possibly non-validating, resolver and so lose DNSSEC's protection. EDE helps expose the real reason.

EDE information is unauthenticated unless secured by a secured DNS transaction such as TSIG, SIG(0), DNS over DTLS or DNS over HTTPS. An attacker, such as a man in the middle or a malicious recursive server, could insert a fake EDE. So EDE content should be treated only as diagnostic information and MUST NOT alter DNS protocol processing. The RFC points out that an attacker who could fake a DNSSEC Bogus EDE could just as easily reply with a fictitious address record, and that RCODEs are no better authenticated.

EDE can also leak information. The Prohibited code (18), for example, may reveal that a name is on a blocklist.
sections.eli5: The note could be forged by a prankster, so treat it like a hint to help fix things, never as proof.

fields.name: OPTION-LENGTH
fields.desc: Octets after this field; should be 2 plus the EXTRA-TEXT length.

fields.name: INFO-CODE
fields.desc: Index into the Extended DNS Errors registry.

items.label: Other
items.desc: Fits no known code; include EXTRA-TEXT.

items.label: Stale Answer
items.desc: Answered from cached data after failing to resolve in time.

items.label: DNSSEC Bogus
items.desc: DNSSEC validation ended in the Bogus state.

items.label: Signature Expired
items.desc: No signatures are presently valid and some are expired.

items.label: Blocked
items.desc: Domain is on a blocklist due to the operator's internal policy.

items.label: Censored
items.desc: Domain is on a blocklist due to an external requirement.

items.label: Filtered
items.desc: Domain is on a blocklist as requested by the client.

items.label: Prohibited
items.desc: Query from an unauthorized client was refused.

items.label: No Reachable Authority
items.desc: None of the authoritative name servers could be reached.
